name: lucky-commit
why: Brute-forces git commit hashes to match a pattern, a fun hash-collision toy that shows how hashes can be steered.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line tool called lucky_commit that rewrites the most recent git commit so its hash starts with a prefix you choose. It takes a hex prefix as an argument (default 0000000) and may include _ placeholders that match any hex character. It works by adding whitespace characters to the commit message and retrying until the resulting SHA1 hash matches. The output is the same commit with a new message and a hash beginning with the requested prefix.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives the framing as 'Make your git commits lucky!' and 'With this simple tool, you can change the start of your git commit hashes to whatever you want.' It offers no deeper rationale; its Why section is just the shrug emoticon.
brief.how_it_works: lucky-commit amends the commit message by inserting a few characters of different whitespace types, then keeps trying new variants until the hash matches. Hashing runs on a GPU through OpenCL by default, with a multithreaded CPU fallback. For non-GPG-signed commits it caches the SHA1 buffer state so each attempt hashes only one 64-byte block; for GPG-signed commits the whitespace goes at the end of the signature, which makes each attempt slower.

commands_seen.context: Run with no arguments to rewrite the latest commit so its hash starts with 0000000 (the default prefix).
Pass a desired hash prefix as a command-line argument; afterwards git log shows the commit hash beginning 1010101.
The _ placeholder means that slot may be any hex character, so the hash must start 00 then any character then 111.
Standard install from crates.io via cargo; the README says this usually puts the binary on your PATH.
Install without OpenCL, falling back to the multithreaded CPU implementation; the README's suggested fix for the '-lOpenCL' linker error.
Build from a cloned source tree; the binary appears at target/release/lucky_commit (lucky_commit.exe on Windows).
Measures how fast the hashing runs on your machine so you can estimate the average search time.
Used before and after running the tool to see the commit hash change.
Installs from the Arch Linux extra repository.
Installs from the default Homebrew tap.

brief.install_notes: You need rustc and cargo, with install instructions linked from the README. By default it links against system OpenCL headers and expects a GPU; if the build fails with 'cannot find -lOpenCL', add --no-default-features to the cargo command. The README says this is the recommended route for a stable build if you don't need GPU speed. OpenCL driver installation varies by OS and only helps if you have a GPU. Distro packages exist for Arch (pacman), Funtoo (emerge dev-util/lucky-commit), and Homebrew. No accounts or first-run configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: Instead of changing the commit's content, it searches over invisible whitespace in the message, so the hash changes while the visible text stays the same. The README also explains the speedup from caching SHA1 state over the 64-byte-aligned tail of the message, and gives a benchmark for estimating time on your machine.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release dates, changelog, or last-commit information, and I did not fetch the repository's commit or release pages. The README does say the older Node.js, C, and pure-Rust branches are unmaintained, but says nothing about the current version. The Arch and Homebrew packaging suggests it is at least in distribution.
brief.caveats: It rewrites the latest commit, so it is a history rewrite; use it on commits you can amend. GPG-signed commits are much slower, and the README says the search time scales with commit message length. Without a GPU the CPU path is about 20x slower by the author's laptop measurement. The OpenCL build can fail to link on systems without OpenCL libraries. The sha256 repository mode is described as experimental. The scout note calls it a 'hash-collision toy', but the README describes prefix brute-forcing by whitespace padding, not collisions. The README's stated timing (about 0.18 s average on the author's 2021 MacBook Pro for 0000000) is the author's own estimate.
quotes: With this simple tool, you can change the start of your git commit hashes to whatever you want.
lucky-commit amends your commit messages by adding a few characters of various types of whitespace, and keeps trying new messages until it finds a good hash.
This is the recommended approach if you just want a stable build, and you don't need the extra performance from GPUs.
fetch_log: https://github.com/not-an-aardvark/lucky-commit — fetched OK; README returned in full, which was sufficient, so no further links were followed.

judge.reason: A surprising demo of steering Git commit hashes with invisible whitespace, and the SHA-1 optimization makes the mechanism worth exploring.

entry.title: lucky-commit
entry.tldr: Rewrites your latest git commit so its hash starts with a prefix you pick, by quietly padding the message with invisible whitespace.
entry.deeper_look:
lucky_commit takes the most recent commit and amends it so the hash begins with a hex prefix of your choosing. With no argument the prefix is 0000000. You can also use `_` as a wildcard, so `00_111` means two zeros, any hex character, then three ones. The visible commit message does not change.

The trick is that a git commit hash is just a SHA1 over the commit's contents, and the message is part of those contents. The tool appends a few characters of different kinds of whitespace, hashes the result, and tries again until the hash matches. The README puts it this way: "lucky-commit amends your commit messages by adding a few characters of various types of whitespace, and keeps trying new messages until it finds a good hash."

Speed comes from two things. Hashing runs on the GPU through OpenCL by default, with a multithreaded CPU fallback. For commits that are not GPG-signed, it caches the SHA1 state up to the final 64-byte block, so each attempt hashes only that one block. Signed commits are slower, because the whitespace goes at the end of the signature.

Underneath it is a small lesson in what a hash does and does not promise. Hashes identify content, but anyone who can vary a harmless part of that content can steer the first few hex digits. Short prefixes are cheap to search for, and each extra digit multiplies the work by 16. That is why a short hash on its own is a weak mark of authenticity.
entry.install:
brew install lucky-commit
# Alternative: cargo install lucky_commit --locked
# If the cargo build fails with 'cannot find -lOpenCL', add --no-default-features to use the CPU path.

try_this.what_happens: Rewrites the latest commit so its hash starts with 0000000. Run `git log` before and after to see the change.
Searches for a hash starting 00, then any hex character, then 111.
Measures hashing speed on your machine so you can estimate how long a given prefix will take.

entry.whats_unique: It leaves the visible commit untouched and searches over invisible whitespace in the message instead. It is also fast enough, with GPU hashing and cached SHA1 state, that short prefixes come back almost instantly.
entry.caveats: It rewrites history, so only use it on a commit you can amend; GPG-signed commits and long messages are slower, and the CPU path is about 20x slower than the GPU by the author's own measurement.
